title: An 18-Year-Old from Ranchi Just Broke Open India's Biggest Exam Scandal
excerpt: Sarthak Sidhant exposed critical failures in the CBSE's On-Screen Marking system. Over four lakh students have since applied for re-evaluation.
body:
An 18-year-old student from Ranchi has done what India's education regulators could not — or would not. Sarthak Sidhant has exposed critical vulnerabilities in the Central Board of Secondary Education's On-Screen Marking system, triggering a political firestorm that now reaches from Parliament's Standing Committee to Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's office.

On Sunday, Gandhi shared a video of his meeting with Sidhant, held in Delhi on June 2, in which the student methodically walked through his findings. Gandhi called it "a victory of youth over government" and said the 18-year-old proved faster than the CBI.

How It Started

After receiving unexpectedly low marks in his Class 12 board exams this year, Sidhant requested scanned copies of his answer sheets for re-evaluation. What he found alarmed him: evidence of incorrect mark deductions, mismatched handwriting on uploaded answer sheets, and systemic glitches in the On-Screen Marking portal run by a Hyderabad-based company called COEMPT Edutek Private Limited.

An ethical hacker named Nisarg Adhikari shared a portal vulnerability with Sidhant through a group chat. Sidhant investigated further and discovered that COEMPT's platform had a history of glitches across multiple universities. He began documenting the irregularities and publishing them on social media.

The findings snowballed. Sidhant has now presented a 500-page dossier before Parliament's Standing Committee on Education, laying out his evidence for systemic failures in the exam evaluation process.

The Scandal Deepens

The CBSE's choice of COEMPT as its technology vendor has come under intense scrutiny. Media reports revealed that COEMPT barely edged out Tata Consultancy Services in the technical assessment but won the contract with a significantly cheaper financial bid. Two cybersecurity certificates submitted by COEMPT to satisfy tender requirements were allegedly tied to other clients — one had expired nearly two years before submission, and the other was audited as a temporary, not production, application.

Gen-Z ethical hackers had flagged critical security flaws in the system as early as February 2025. The CBSE denied the issues until it could no longer do so.

In what Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh called "a final admission that COEMPT's portal was irretrievably compromised," the board has now shifted all Class 12 answer-sheet data from COEMPT's servers to its own infrastructure. IIT Kanpur and IIT Madras teams have been brought in to conduct a full security audit, deploying "red team" and "blue team" approaches to test the system's resilience.

Over Four Lakh Students Apply for Re-checking

The scale of the fallout is staggering. More than 400,000 students have applied for re-checking of their scanned answer sheets — a number that speaks to the depth of mistrust the scandal has generated. Cases of students receiving significantly higher marks after re-evaluation have raised fundamental questions about whether errors were widespread during the original assessment.

The CBSE extended its re-evaluation deadline by one day to June 7, after students reported difficulty accessing their answer sheets through the post-result services portal. Sidhant himself asked for the extension with characteristic directness, posting on X: "Can u please extend the deadline please because I was busy this week exposing you."

Political Fallout

The Congress has called for Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. Ramesh accused him of running "a deeply compromised Ministry" and described his continuation in office as speaking only "to his shameless desire for power."

The BJP has so far defended the minister, but the optics are difficult. The CBSE's own actions — migrating data to its own servers, bringing in IIT teams, extending deadlines — amount to a tacit acknowledgment that the original system was not fit for purpose.

What It Means for NRI Families

For Indian diaspora families who maintain connections with India's education system — whether through children studying in India, planning to take competitive exams, or evaluating Indian qualifications for overseas applications — the scandal raises uncomfortable questions about institutional credibility. The CBSE board exam is one of the most consequential assessments in Indian education, directly shaping access to undergraduate admissions and, by extension, career trajectories.

The controversy also underscores a broader pattern: India's examination infrastructure, from NEET to CBSE, has faced repeated integrity crises in recent years, eroding confidence in systems that affect tens of millions of students annually.

Sidhant, for his part, framed his work simply. "This is our country," he told Gandhi. "Everyone should have enough civic sense to read things and work towards making the system transparent."
